locator: Letter of October 11, 2023, answer to question 3, page 3
shows: In a service letter of October 11, 2023, LADWP states that the maximum treatment capacity of the Los Angeles Aqueduct Filtration Plant (LAAFP) is 600 million gallons a day. The average flow through the plant was 333 million gallons a day in 2023 to the date of the letter. LADWP has no plans to expand the plant. Its other supplies are the Metropolitan Water District, recycled water and groundwater wells.
limits: One plant: the capacity leaves out LADWP's wells and groundwater treatment plants. It is a treatment capacity, and the plant can treat only the water that reaches it from the Los Angeles Aqueduct and from untreated purchases, so its output can be less. The letter answers a developer's question and gives no rating method.

locator: Water Supply, 'Sources of Water Supply', table 'Water Supply and Demand (In Acre-Feet)', printed p. 40; Los Angeles Aqueduct, printed p. 36
shows: LADWP's 2025 bond statement gives its water supply and demand for fiscal years 2020 to 2024 (years ended June 30), in acre-feet. Total demand was 487,591, 508,359, 500,743, 441,855 and 448,358, and it includes recycled water of 9,641, 11,455, 12,022, 9,428 and 10,030. limits: Fiscal-year totals reported by the utility; they give no highest day, so the scenario applies the median peak ratio of the systems that report one. The supply and demand totals differ by water put into or taken from storage. Recycled water goes to non-potable uses through its own pipes and is taken out here. The five years include drought years and the wet year 2023-24; the scenario year can differ.

locator: The Water System, 'Storage', printed p. 37, and table 'Current Storage Capacity', printed p. 38; 'Water Treatment Facilities - Disinfection', printed p. 39
shows: LADWP's 124 storage tanks and reservoirs hold about 323,000 acre-feet, and eight aqueduct reservoirs hold about 96% of it. The storage table lists the aqueduct reservoirs (310,542 acre-feet, 101,190 million gallons) apart from the local reservoirs in the city. The local reservoirs total 13,056 acre-feet: Los Angeles Reservoir 10,170, nine other named reservoirs 2,152, and 106 smaller reservoirs and tanks 734. The table prints the local total as 4,240 million gallons; its own million-gallon column adds to 4,255. The statement says that all of the system's reservoirs now meet the rules that protect drinking water stored in reservoirs, and that the outflow of Los Angeles Reservoir gets ultraviolet treatment again before it enters the pipes.
limits: Gross capacities at the spillway, not usable volumes. Los Angeles Reservoir is 78% of the local total (10,170 of 13,056 acre-feet); its outflow goes through an ultraviolet plant, which has controls of its own. Without it the local reservoirs hold 2,886 acre-feet (derived). The aqueduct reservoirs hold untreated water and are left out. Four emergency reservoirs (24,386 acre-feet) not in use are also left out.

shows: Metropolitan's capacity charge for 2025 uses each member agency's peak day demand on Metropolitan's system from May 1 to September 30. limits: The highest day of deliveries from Metropolitan in the summer months only, not the highest day of LADWP's total use and not a contract capacity; the capacity of the connections is not given. The years 2021 and 2022 were dry, when LADWP bought more from Metropolitan.
